title: Ionic Reactions and Tests for Ions
lines: Reactions in water are really reactions between ions. This topic asks you to write correct ionic equations, judge whether a group of ions can stay together in one solution, and pick the right test for an ion. Each skill rests on knowing which substances are strong electrolytes and which compounds are insoluble.
## Electrolytes and non-electrolytes
- An electrolyte is a compound that conducts electricity when molten or dissolved in water, because it forms mobile ions. Acids, bases, salts and metal oxides (when molten) are electrolytes.
- Non-electrolytes do not conduct in either state: sucrose, ethanol, most organic compounds, and non-metal oxides such as CO₂, SO₂ and NH₃.

- Strong electrolytes ionise completely in water: strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, H₂SO₄, HNO₃, HClO₄), strong bases (NaOH, KOH, Ba(OH)₂, Ca(OH)₂) and almost all salts, including insoluble ones like BaSO₄.
- Weak electrolytes ionise only partly: weak acids (CH₃COOH, H₂CO₃, H₂SO₃, H₂S, HClO, HF, H₃PO₄), weak bases (NH₃·H₂O, insoluble hydroxides) and water.
- Ionisation equations: NaHSO₄ → Na⁺ + H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ (in water); NaHCO₃ → Na⁺ + HCO₃⁻; CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺.

! Trap: CO₂ dissolved in water conducts, but the conducting species come from H₂CO₃; CO₂ itself is a non-electrolyte. Copper and salt water conduct but are not electrolytes, because electrolytes must be compounds, and salt water is a mixture.
! Trap: conductivity depends on ion concentration and charge, not on whether the electrolyte is strong. A very dilute HCl solution can conduct worse than a concentrated acetic acid solution.
> Example: Ba(OH)₂ solution is titrated with dilute H₂SO₄. How does the conductivity change?
> Ba²⁺ + 2OH⁻ + 2H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄↓ + 2H₂O removes almost all ions, so the bulb dims to nearly zero at the equivalence point, then brightens again as excess H₂SO₄ adds ions.
## Writing ionic equations
- Write: the balanced full equation. Split: only soluble strong electrolytes into ions. Cancel: spectator ions that appear unchanged on both sides. Check: atoms and charge both balance.
- Keep as formulas: precipitates, gases, water and other weak electrolytes, oxides, elements, and organic molecules.
- Ca(OH)₂: as clear limewater write Ca²⁺ + 2OH⁻; as lime milk (suspension) write Ca(OH)₂.
- Concentrated H₂SO₄ is written as a formula; concentrated HCl and HNO₃ are written as ions.
> Example: Write the ionic equation for marble dissolving in hydrochloric acid.
> CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂↑. CaCO₃ is insoluble and stays as a formula; Cl⁻ cancels.
> CaCO₃ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + H₂O + CO₂↑.
> Example: Ionic equation for acetic acid neutralising sodium hydroxide.
> CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O. Acetic acid is weak, so it is not written as H⁺.
## Common errors in ionic equations
- Breaking a weak electrolyte or a precipitate: writing H⁺ for CH₃COOH, or Ca²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ for CaCO₃.
- Unbalanced charge: Fe³⁺ + Cu → Fe²⁺ + Cu²⁺ looks balanced in atoms but has charge +3 on the left and +4 on the right. Correct: 2Fe³⁺ + Cu → 2Fe²⁺ + Cu²⁺.
- Wrong ratio: Ba²⁺ + OH⁻ + H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄↓ + H₂O is wrong; the formulas demand 2OH⁻ and 2H⁺ for each Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻.
- Impossible product: Fe + 2H⁺ → Fe²⁺ + H₂↑ is right; writing Fe³⁺ is wrong for non-oxidising acids. Cu + 2H⁺ → Cu²⁺ + H₂↑ does not happen at all.
- Ignoring amounts: with a small amount of CO₂, 2OH⁻ + CO₂ → CO₃²⁻ + H₂O; with excess CO₂, OH⁻ + CO₂ → HCO₃⁻.

- With amount-dependent reactions, let the limiting reagent have coefficient 1. NaHCO₃ with a little Ca(OH)₂: Ca²⁺ + 2OH⁻ + 2HCO₃⁻ → CaCO₃↓ + CO₃²⁻ + 2H₂O. NaHCO₃ with excess Ca(OH)₂: HCO₃⁻ + Ca²⁺ + OH⁻ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂O.
! Trap: ClO⁻ is strongly oxidising. SO₂ passed into Ca(ClO)₂ solution does not give CaSO₃; it is oxidised to sulfate (CaSO₄).
## Conditions for ionic reactions
- Double-displacement ionic reactions go when they form a precipitate, a gas or a weak electrolyte (including water), because these remove ions from solution.
- Redox reactions between ions also go: 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂.
- Complex formation also removes ions: Fe³⁺ + 3SCN⁻ → Fe(SCN)₃ (blood-red).
- Two hydrolysing ions can drive each other to completion: Al³⁺ + 3HCO₃⁻ → Al(OH)₃↓ + 3CO₂↑ (foam fire extinguisher).
## Ion coexistence in solution
- Ions cannot coexist if they form a precipitate (Ba²⁺ with SO₄²⁻ or CO₃²⁻; Ag⁺ with Cl⁻; Ca²⁺ with CO₃²⁻; OH⁻ with Mg²⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe³⁺, Al³⁺).
- If they form a gas or weak electrolyte (H⁺ with CO₃²⁻, HCO₃⁻, SO₃²⁻, S²⁻, CH₃COO⁻, ClO⁻; OH⁻ with NH₄⁺; H⁺ with OH⁻).
- HCO₃⁻ and HSO₃⁻ cannot exist in either strongly acidic or strongly basic solution: HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ → CO₃²⁻ + H₂O.
- If they react by redox: in acid, NO₃⁻ oxidises Fe²⁺, I⁻, SO₃²⁻ and S²⁻; MnO₄⁻ oxidises Fe²⁺, I⁻ and Cl⁻; Fe³⁺ oxidises I⁻ and S²⁻; ClO⁻ oxidises Fe²⁺ and I⁻.
- If they form a complex: Fe³⁺ with SCN⁻.

- Hidden conditions: "colourless" rules out Cu²⁺ (blue), Fe³⁺ (yellow-brown), Fe²⁺ (pale green) and MnO₄⁻ (purple). "pH = 1" or "turns litmus red" means extra H⁺. "pH = 13" or "turns phenolphthalein red" means extra OH⁻. "Reacts with Al to give H₂" means acid or base (and in acid, no NO₃⁻, since HNO₃ gives no H₂).
> Example: Which group can coexist in a colourless solution at pH = 1: (A) Na⁺, K⁺, MnO₄⁻, SO₄²⁻ (B) NH₄⁺, Mg²⁺, NO₃⁻, Cl⁻ (C) Fe²⁺, H⁺, NO₃⁻, Cl⁻ (D) K⁺, Na⁺, CO₃²⁻, Cl⁻?
> A has purple MnO₄⁻, so it is not colourless. C: NO₃⁻ with H⁺ oxidises Fe²⁺ (and Fe²⁺ is coloured). D: CO₃²⁻ reacts with H⁺. B has no reacting pair, so B is correct.
! Trap: NO₃⁻ is harmless in neutral solution; it only becomes a strong oxidant together with H⁺. Watch for this pair in every coexistence question.
## Tests for anions
- Cl⁻: add dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃ solution; a white precipitate of AgCl that does not dissolve. HNO₃ removes CO₃²⁻ that would otherwise also give a white precipitate.
- SO₄²⁻: first add dilute HCl (no precipitate, no gas, which rules out Ag⁺, CO₃²⁻ and SO₃²⁻), then BaCl₂ solution; white BaSO₄ forms.
- CO₃²⁻: add dilute HCl; a colourless, odourless gas turns limewater cloudy. To tell CO₃²⁻ from HCO₃⁻, add CaCl₂ or BaCl₂ solution: only CO₃²⁻ gives a precipitate.
- SO₃²⁻ with acid gives SO₂, which also clouds limewater but has a choking smell and decolourises magenta (fuchsine) solution.
- Br⁻ and I⁻: AgNO₃ gives pale yellow AgBr and yellow AgI. Or add chlorine water, then CCl₄: the lower layer turns orange-red for Br₂ and purple for I₂.

! Trap: adding acidified Ba(NO₃)₂ to test for SO₄²⁻ is wrong, because HNO₃ oxidises SO₃²⁻ to SO₄²⁻ and gives a false positive. Adding BaCl₂ first and acid after is also wrong, because AgCl would look the same as BaSO₄.
## Tests for cations
- NH₄⁺: add NaOH solution and warm; a gas with a pungent smell turns moist red litmus blue (NH₃). Without warming, little NH₃ escapes from dilute solutions.
- Fe³⁺: KSCN solution turns blood-red. Or NaOH gives a red-brown Fe(OH)₃ precipitate.

- Fe²⁺: KSCN shows no colour; then add chlorine water (or H₂O₂) and the solution turns red (2Fe²⁺ + Cl₂ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2Cl⁻). Or NaOH gives a white precipitate that turns grey-green and finally red-brown. Fe²⁺ also decolourises acidified KMnO₄, which is the test when Fe³⁺ is also present. Another specific test is K₃[Fe(CN)₆], which gives a blue precipitate with Fe²⁺.
- Cu²⁺: blue solution; NaOH gives a blue Cu(OH)₂ precipitate.
- Al³⁺: NaOH gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess. Mg²⁺: white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess.
- Flame tests (clean Pt or iron wire, dipped in HCl and burnt until colourless first): Na⁺ yellow; K⁺ lilac, seen through blue cobalt glass to filter out sodium's yellow.
> Example: A solution may contain Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺ or both. Describe a two-step test.
> Take one portion and add KSCN: red means Fe³⁺ present. Take a second portion and add a few drops of acidified KMnO₄: if the purple colour fades, Fe²⁺ is present.
! Trap: for Fe²⁺, the order matters. Add KSCN first, then the oxidant. Adding chlorine water first cannot tell you whether the Fe³⁺ was there from the start.
